results.title: Climate change, risks and ECB strategy: what is the effect on European banks’ stock return? | Risk Management | Springer Nature Link

Title: Climate change, risks and ECB strategy: what is the effect on European banks’ stock return? | Risk Management | Springer Nature Link
These results contribute to the understanding of how climate-related ECB communications interact with financial markets and bank stock returns, offering insights for investors assessing climate policy, for banks in managing climate-related risks, and for policymakers designing effective communication strategies. This paper advances the state of the art by exploring whether ECB announcements concerning climate change related-stress tests generate abnormal stock returns among European banks. Annals of Finance 21:1–17.")) provide one of the first empirical assessments of market reactions to the ECB’s 2021 economy-wide climate stress test, focusing on euro area banks and non-financial corporations. Their event study analysis reveals three key findings: (i) the first announcement of the stress test methodology does not elicit significant market reactions, due to the qualitative nature of the information disclosed; (ii) the release of final results triggers a significant positive market reaction, suggesting that market participants anticipate outcomes; and (iii) global climate-related events, such as the opening of COP26, has no significant impact on bank stock prices. Using an event study and a dataset combining banks with regional indicators of climate-related physical risk (floods, landslides, and extreme temperatures), the authors show that investors react negatively to both the test’s announcement and the publication of its results, even if no direct impact on regulatory capital and no detailed disclosure for individual institutions occur. Statistically significant abnormal returns around the announcement date highlight the ECB’s credible and assertive commitment to climate-related supervision and the different response from European banks rather than banks in the Eurozone or SIs. In contrast, the third announcement event window (November 22, 2021), which present the ECB’s assessment of banks’ progress in managing climate risks, generates negative and statistically significant CRARs. This indicates somewhat of investor scepticism regarding the effectiveness of the ECB’s review and concern over the sector’s lack of preparedness, especially in the absence of immediate regulatory consequences. The fifth announcement, related to the publication of climate stress test results, triggers strong anticipatory reactions, especially among Eurozone banks and SIs. These findings are robust across different specifications of abnormal return as mean-adjusted returns (MAR), and market-adjusted returns (MKAR).

results.title: ECB Prioritizes Climate, Nature Risks in Financial Strategy Shift - The Financial Analyst
results.content: The European Central Bank (ECB) has unveiled a series of new priority areas to deepen its work on integrating climate and nature-related risks into its activities, signaling a significant shift in its approach to addressing the economic and financial impacts of the climate crisis. The ECB’s new priorities reflect a heightened focus on three key areas: the transition to a green economy, coping with the growing physical impacts of climate change on the economy and financial system, and the impact of nature-related risks and ecosystem degradation. The ECB’s new priorities are a significant step forward in addressing the economic and financial consequences of climate change and nature degradation. As the central bank noted, “The economic and financial consequences of climate change and nature degradation continue to grow.” By intensifying its work in these key areas, the ECB is taking a proactive approach to mitigating these risks and ensuring the stability and resilience of the financial system. The ECB’s new priorities also highlight the increasing recognition of the role that central banks and financial regulators can play in addressing the challenges posed by climate change and nature degradation. As the ECB noted, “The ECB needs to account for the effects of climate change and nature degradation in the conduct of its tasks within its mandate.” By embedding climate and nature-related risks into its core work, the ECB is setting an example for other central banks and financial regulators around the world. In conclusion, the ECB’s new priorities represent a significant step forward in addressing the economic and financial consequences of climate change and nature degradation. By focusing on the transition to a green economy, coping with the growing physical impacts of climate change, and addressing the impact of nature-related risks and ecosystem degradation, the ECB is taking a proactive approach to mitigating these risks and ensuring the stability and resilience of the financial system. The ECB’s new priorities also highlight the increasing recognition of the role that central banks and financial regulators can play in addressing the challenges posed by climate change and nature degradation, and set an example for other central banks and financial regulators around the world.
